citation.quote: The second portion of this Counter-Criticism u as published under the NOM DE PLUME of G. Edward in the fourth 1847 issue of Otto Wigand's review THE EPIGIDNES as "The reactionary philosophers. A reply to Kuno Fischer's The Modern Sophists"

title: Kuno Fischer publishes The Modern Sophists
summary: Kuno Fischer's criticism of Stirner, "The Modern Sophists," appeared in the Leipziger Revue and was essentially directed against him.

citation.quote: Stirner replied to a criticism from Kuno Fischer, which had appeared in 1847 as "The Modern Sophists," in the LEIPZIGER REVUE and which was essentially directed against him.

title: Marx publishes The Poverty of Philosophy
summary: Karl Marx published The Poverty of Philosophy as a reply to Proudhon's System of Economic Contradictions.

citation.quote: Systeme des contradictions ekonomi ques ou Philosophic de la misere, two vols., 1846, to which Marx was to reply the following year with his Poverty of Philosophy.

title: Birth of Sergei Netchayev
summary: Sergei Netchayev, the young Russian revolutionary who influenced Bakunin, was born.

citation.quote: Sergei Netchayev (1847–1882), a young Russian revolutionary.

title: Proudhon enters revolutionary arena in 1848
summary: The 1848 revolution gave Proudhon the opportunity to step into the revolutionary arena, after which the subversive boldness of his writings under the second Bonaparte earned him harassment, imprisonment and exile.

citation.quote: The 1848 revolution provided him with an opportunity to step, not without courage, into the revolutionary arena, and under the second Bonaparte, the subversive boldness of his writings earned him harassment, imprisonment and exile.

title: Republic given 'three months to eliminate poverty'
summary: Proudhon recalls the 1848 Republic, when workers took up the slogan 'Live by working or die fighting!' and demanded the Republic eliminate poverty in three months, later scrawling 'Bread or lead!' on their banners by June.

citation.quote: I was one of that breed which, a little later, took up the slogan of Live by working or die fighting! which, in 1848, gave the Republic three months to eliminate poverty and, come June, scribbled Bread or lead! upon their banners.

title: Louis Bonaparte elected to the National Assembly
summary: In the by-elections following the June Days, Prince Louis Bonaparte, nephew of Napoleon, was elected by 300,000 votes across five departments — riding the conservative reaction.

citation.quote: Except in the Seine department, the by-elections had favored the conservatives and a newcomer, Prince Louis Bonaparte, nephew of the great Napoleon, who successfully had himself returned by 300,000 votes across five departments.

title: Louis Blanc preaches state socialism from the Luxembourg Commission
summary: During the 1848 Revolution, Louis Blanc advocated a statist, 'communistic' socialism from the so-called Luxembourg Commission — the target of Proudhon's polemic in this chapter.

citation.quote: Here, in retrospect, Proudhon attacks the type of State and "communistic" socialism preached by Louis Blanc during the t8y8 Revolution from the so-called Luxembourg Commission.

title: Publication of the Communist Manifesto
summary: Marx and Engels set out in the 1848 Communist Manifesto their idea of proletarian revolution in stages, beginning with capture of political power and centralization of production in State hands.

citation.chapter: BAKUNIN AND MARX ON THE COMMUNE
citation.quote: In the Address, better known under the name The Civil War in France, Marx overhauled certain passages of the 1848 Communist Manifesto. Marx and Engels, the authors of that illustrious document, had set out therein their idea of proletarian revolution in stages.

title: Bakunin reads the Communist Manifesto in German
summary: Unlike the French socialists, Bakunin was conversant with the Communist Manifesto in the German original from 1848 and criticized its two-stage statist conception of revolution.

citation.chapter: BAKUNIN AND MARX ON THE COMMUNE
citation.quote: Bakunin who, unlike the French socialists, had been conversant with the Communist Manifesto, in the German original since 1848, had not missed an opportunity to criticize this splitting of the revolution into two stages, the first of which would still be emphatically statist.

title: Guillaume family returns to Switzerland after Neuchatel republic proclaimed
summary: After a Republic was proclaimed in Neuchatel in 1848, James Guillaume's enthusiastic republican father returned to Switzerland, where he was soon appointed a judge, then prefect of the Val-de-Travers.

citation.quote: In 1848, after a Republic was proclaimed in Neuchatel, James Guillaume's father, himself an enthusiastic republican, returned to Switzerland. He was soon appointed a judge, then prefect of the Val-de-Travers, and from then on concentrated exclusively upon public life.

title: February Revolution erupts in France
summary: The popular explosion of February 1848 overthrew the July Monarchy and ushered in the Second Republic, an event Proudhon initially dreaded but soon welcomed.

citation.quote: Prior to the popular explosion in February, he had been nothing short of reticent. He could sense that the monarchy was approaching its end, but he did nothing to speed its demise.

title: February Revolution cited as precedent
summary: Marx and Engels cited the practical experiences of the February 1848 revolution as supporting the need to revise the Communist Manifesto.

citation.chapter: BAKUNIN AND MARX ON THE COMMUNE
citation.quote: And, remarkably, they cited in support of any such redrafting "the practical experiences, first of the February [1848] revolution, then, to a much greater extent, of the Paris Commune, when, for the first time, the proletariat held political power in its hands over a two month period."

title: February 1848 insurrection establishes Republic
summary: The Republic emerged naturally from the February 1848 insurrection, the product of thirty years of conspiratorial work by republican secret societies under the Restoration and Louis-Philippe.

citation.quote: If the Republic emerged quite naturally from the February 1848 insurrection, this was thanks to these societies, thanks to the propaganda by deed which they had mounted over those thirty years.

title: Parisian revolution of February 1848
summary: The Parisian revolution of February 1848 overthrew the July Monarchy and established a provisional government.

citation.quote: reference to the Pansian revolution of February 1848.

title: Proclamation of the Republic; Raspail marches on city hall
summary: François-Vincent Raspail was one of the first to march on the Paris city hall and proclaim the Republic on February 24, 1848, the date Proudhon associated with the revolution he himself had not pushed.

citation.quote: I would not have made the revolution of February 24: but the people's instinct has decided otherwise.... I stand by them all.

title: Bakunin arrives in Paris during February Revolution
summary: Mikhail Bakunin, a Russian emigre, traveled to Paris upon hearing of the fighting, arriving three days after the proclamation of the Republic.

citation.chapter: THE REVOLUTION OF FEBRUARY 1848, AS SEEN BY BAKUNIN'
citation.quote: I was obliged to make a detour, the railway being impassable in a number of places, and I arrived in Paris on February 26, within three days of the proclamation of the Republic.

title: Trades demonstration leads to Luxembourg Commission
summary: Following a demonstration by trades bodies outside the Paris city hall, the provisional government launched a 'Government commission for workers' housed in the Luxembourg Palace and chaired by Louis Blanc.

citation.quote: Following a demonstration by trades bodies outside the city hall on 28 February 1848, the provisional government launched a "Government commission for workers," housed in the Luxembourg Palace and chaired by Louis Blanc

title: Luxembourg Commission's working period
summary: The Luxembourg Commission carried out its work between March 1 and May 16, 1848, ultimately drafting labor organization and social legislation plans.

citation.quote: The work of the commission was carried out during the period between March 1 and May 16. In the end, it ventured to draw up a labor organization plan and drafted the social legislation which was subsequently promulgated by the provisional government.

title: Louis Blanc organizes mass demonstration of 100,000 workers
summary: On 17 March 1848 Louis Blanc helped organize a huge popular demonstration of more than 100,000 workers in Paris, but kept it from challenging the government — a failure Proudhon never forgave.

citation.quote: On 17 March 1848, Louis Blanc had been one of the organizers of a huge popular demonstration that had attracted upwards of 100,000 workers. But he had prevented its being turned into a gauntlet thrown down to the government to compel it to take a more vigorous line with regard to those sabotaging the Revolution.

title: Proudhon defeated in April elections
summary: Proudhon ran for office in the April 1848 elections to the National Assembly but was defeated.

citation.quote: Defeated at first in the April elections, he was returned as a deputy in the follow-up elections on June 4-5, 1848, by some 77, 000 votes.

title: Proudhon's circular to voters in the Doubs
summary: In an electoral circular dated April 3, 1848 addressed to the voters in the Doubs, Proudhon called for reconciliation between workers and employers around the social question.

citation.quote: (...) Along came the April elections. I deluded myself into running as a candidate. In the circular that I addressed to the voters in the Doubs, dated April 3, 1848, I stated:

title: April 16 ends Proudhon's first candidacy
summary: The events of April 16, 1848 in Paris dashed Proudhon's prospects as a candidate and turned opinion against extreme radicalism.

citation.quote: April 16 put paid to my prospects as candidate. After that dismal day, people wanted to hear no more about extreme radicalism: they preferred to compromise everything by throwing themselves into the embrace of extreme conservatism.

title: Storming of the Palais Bourbon; Raspail arrested
summary: On May 15, 1848 the popular clubs led by Raspail and Blanqui stormed the Palais Bourbon, declared the assembly dissolved, and briefly installed an insurgent government before Raspail was arrested and imprisoned at Vincennes.

citation.quote: Alongside Auguste Blanqui, he had been one of the leading lights behind the mighty demonstration by the popular clubs which had stormed into the Palais Bourbon on May 15, declaring the assembly dissolved and installing a short-lived insurgent government in the city hall. That same evening, along with Barbs and a handful of others, Raspail had been arrested and committed to the Vincennes fortress.

title: June Days uprising and Cavaignac's repression
summary: A fortnight after Proudhon's election, the Paris workers rose against the closure of the National Workshops. The Faubourg Saint-Antoine revolt was savagely crushed by General Cavaignac's troops.

citation.quote: A fortnight later, the workers from the faubourgs rose up to register their protest at the closure of the "national workshops," a sort of work scheme that had been devised for the purpose of reducing unemployment.

title: Cavaignac suppresses the Parisian proletariat
summary: General Cavaignac led the bloody repression of the Parisian workers' insurrection in June 1848.

citation.quote: General Louis-Eugene Cavaignac (1802–1857), the butcher of the conquest of Algeria and later butcher of the Parisian proletariat in June 1848.

title: Proudhon elected deputy in by-elections
summary: In the follow-up elections of June 4–5, 1848, Proudhon was returned to the National Assembly with some 77,000 votes.

citation.quote: Defeated at first in the April elections, he was returned as a deputy in the follow-up elections on June 4-5, 1848, by some 77, 000 votes.

title: Proudhon's incendiary speech to the National Assembly
summary: On July 31, 1848 Proudhon defended his bill — a one-third levy on incomes paired with a one-third rent discount — in a provocative Assembly speech, identifying himself with the proletariat against the bourgeois class.

citation.quote: On July 31, Proudhon explained himself in a great speech delivered before the assembly. Exasperated by interruptions and insults, he turned provocateur.

title: Proudhon's revenue bill rejected 691 to 2
summary: Following the July 31 speech, Proudhon's tax-and-rent bill was rejected almost unanimously by the National Assembly, 691 votes to 2 (the two yes votes being Proudhon and a deputy named Greppo).

citation.quote: The scandal created by this parliamentary outburst was tremendous and Proudhon's bill was rejected virtually unanimously by 691 votes to 2, the latter being Proudhon and a certain Greppo.

title: Raspail elected in Seine by-elections from prison
summary: In the by-elections of September 17, 1848, the imprisoned François-Vincent Raspail — endorsed by Proudhon's newspaper Le Peuple — was elected by some 70,000 voters of the Seine department as a protest against the June victors.

citation.quote: The by-elections of September 17, 1848 provided Proudhon with a further opportunity to espouse a clear-cut revolutionary stance. Swallowing his repugnance vis-a-vis universal suffrage yet again, he gave his endorsement through his newspaper to the candidacy of François-Vincent Raspail.

title: Louis Bonaparte elected President of the Republic
summary: In the presidential election of December 10, 1848, Louis Bonaparte defeated Cavaignac, Ledru-Rollin and Raspail by a huge majority, signaling the end of the revolution.

citation.quote: Whereupon he put himself forward as a candidate in the presidential elections of December 10.

title: Proudhon's Confessions d'un révolutionnaire published
summary: Proudhon's Confessions d'un révolutionnaire pour servir à l'histoire de la révolution de Février was published.

citation.quote: from Confessions d'un revolutionnaire pour servir d I'histoire de la revolution de evrier, 1849.

title: Publication of Colin's Socialisme rationnel
summary: Baron Colin's Socialisme rationnel was published.

citation.quote: (Le Pactes social 1835, and Socialisme rationnel 1849)

title: Bakunin participates in Dresden uprising
summary: Galvanized by the 1848 Revolution, Bakunin participated in the popular uprising in Dresden.

citation.chapter: THE REVOLUTION OF FEBRUARY 1848, AS SEEN BY BAKUNIN'
citation.quote: Following his short passage through Paris during the 1848 Revolution, Bakunin, galvanized by the example before his very eyes, shot off to participate in the popular uprising in Dresden (May 3, 1849).

title: Bakunin sentenced to death in Austria
summary: After being sentenced to death in Saxony, Bakunin was sentenced to death again in Austria in 1850, then handed over to Russian government.

citation.chapter: THE REVOLUTION OF FEBRUARY 1848, AS SEEN BY BAKUNIN'
citation.quote: As a result of which he was sentenced to death in Saxony and then in Austria in 1850, being eventually handed over by Austria to the Russian government.

title: Publication of de Potter's Catéchisme social
summary: Louis de Potter published his Catéchisme social.

citation.quote: His chief disciple, Louis de Potter, published, among other things. a Caiecliisme social in 1850.

title: Publication of Proudhon's General Idea of the Revolution
summary: Proudhon's Idée générale de la révolution au XIXe siècle was published.

citation.quote: Extracts lifted from Idee generale de la revolution au XXe siecle, 1851.

title: Louis-Napoleon Bonaparte's coup d'état
summary: Louis-Napoleon Bonaparte (Napoleon III) seized power by coup d'état on December 2, 1851.

citation.quote: Louis-Napoleon Bonaparte (Napoleon III) had seized power by coup d'état on December 2, 1851.

title: Publication of Stirner's History of Reaction
summary: Stirner's two-volume History of Reaction was published in Berlin.

citation.quote: 1852 saw the publication in Berlin of his two-volume History of Reaction.

title: Stirner's translation of Say's Capital and Interest
summary: Stirner's annotated translation of J.B. Say's pamphlet Capital and Interest was published in Hamburg.

citation.quote: Also in 1852, we find his annotated translation of J.B. Say's pamphlet Capital and interest, published in Hamburg.

title: Constitution of the Second Empire promulgated under Napoleon III
summary: Proudhon notes that the Luxembourg communists' profession of faith is in principle in agreement with the 1852 Constitution under Napoleon III, sharing its authoritarian conception of sovereignty.

citation.quote: The Luxembourg communists, the Icarians and all the rest can, with an easy conscience, pledge loyalty to Napoleon III; their profession of faith is, in principle, in agreement with the 1852 Constitution: and is even a lot less.

title: Publication of Proudhon's La Révolution sociale démontrée par le coup d'État
summary: Proudhon's La Révolution sociale démontrée par le coup d'État du 2 décembre was published.

citation.quote: Extract lifted from La Revolution sori ale demontree par le coup d' Etat du 2 dekemhre (1852).

title: Stirner imprisoned for debt
summary: Coping day by day as best he could, Stirner was twice thrown into prison for debt.

citation.quote: In 1853 he was twice thrown into prison for debt.

title: German journalists revive libel against Bakunin
summary: Some German journalists put the old calumny against Bakunin from the Neue Rheinische Zeitung back into circulation in 1853.

citation.chapter: THE REVOLUTION OF FEBRUARY 1848, AS SEEN BY BAKUNIN'
citation.quote: the calumny' once published by the Neue Rheinische Zeitung and put back into circulation by some German journalists in 1853.

title: Guillaume's father elected State Councilor
summary: In 1853, James Guillaume's father was elected State Councilor, a position to which he was returned again and again over a period of thirty-five years.

citation.quote: Elected State Councilor in 1853, he returned again and again over a period of thirty-five years.

title: Errico Malatesta born in Caserta province
summary: Errico Malatesta was born in Italy's Caserta province into a family of modest rural landowners.

citation.quote: Errico Malatesta was born in Italy's Caserta province on December 14, 1853, into a family of modest rural landowners.

title: Death of Adolphe Blanqui
summary: The bourgeois economist Adolphe Blanqui died.

citation.quote: Adolphe Blanqui (1798–1854) a bourgeois economist and brother of the great revolutionary Auguste Blanqui.

title: Death of Max Stirner
summary: Max Stirner, the German individualist philosopher, dies.

citation.quote: MAX STIRNER (1806–1856)

title: Death of Francis Villegardelle
summary: Francis Villegardelle, Fourierist-turned-communist, died.

citation.quote: Francis Villegardelle (1810–1856), at first a Fourierist and later a communist.

title: Death of Étienne Cabet
summary: Étienne Cabet, founder of the Icarian utopian communities in the United States, died.

citation.quote: Etienne Cabet (1788–1856), author of Voyage en Irarie, attempted to launch in the United States.

title: Death of Max Stirner
summary: Max Stirner died from an infection caused by a bite from an anthrax-bearing fly, almost fifty years old. Bruno Bauer and Ludwig Buhl accompanied him on his final pilgrimage.

citation.quote: On June 25, 1856 he died from an infection caused by a bite from an anthrax-bearing fly. His Calvary was at an end. He was almost fifty years old.

title: Previous imperial elections show narrow Paris victory
summary: In the 1857 elections, despite the peasantry's support across most provinces, the regime narrowly won Paris with 110,536 votes against 96,299 for the democratic opposition, returning five liberal deputies including Alfred Darimon.

citation.quote: On which occasion, although the support of the peasantry had been secured in the vast majority of provinces, in Paris the victory had nonetheless been a narrow one: the regime won by 110,536 votes as against the 96,299 for the democratic opposition. Five liberal deputies had thus been returned.

title: Death of General Louis-Eugène Cavaignac
summary: General Louis-Eugène Cavaignac, butcher of the June 1848 Parisian proletariat insurrection, died.

citation.quote: General Louis-Eugene Cavaignac (1802–1857), the butcher of the conquest of Algeria and later butcher of the Parisian proletariat in June 1848.

title: Bakunin writes Confession to the Tsar
summary: Bakunin's Confession, a letter to the Tsar, was written in 1857 (later published in Paris in 1932).

citation.quote: Extracted from Confession (1857 Letter to the Tsar), Paris, 1932.

title: Death of Robert Owen
summary: Robert Owen, English utopian socialist, died.

citation.quote: Robert Owen (1771–1858), English "utopian" socialist

title: War of 1859 in Italy
summary: The war of 1859, mentioned alongside Garibaldi's expedition, marked the beginning of new life in Italy.

citation.chapter: THE REVOLUTION OF FEBRUARY 1848, AS SEEN BY BAKUNIN'
citation.quote: In the wake of the war of 1859 and Garibaldi's heroic expedition in 1860, Italy had just begun a new life

title: Death of Baron Colin
summary: The Baron Colin, collectivist socialist theorist, died.

citation.quote: The Baron Colin (1783–1859)

title: Garibaldi's heroic expedition
summary: Garibaldi's heroic expedition in 1860, alongside the war of 1859, marked the beginning of new life in Italy.

citation.chapter: THE REVOLUTION OF FEBRUARY 1848, AS SEEN BY BAKUNIN'
citation.quote: In the wake of the war of1859 and Garibaldi's heroic expedition in 1860, Italy had just begun a new life

title: Émile Pouget born near Rodez
summary: Émile Pouget was born in 1860 near Rodez in the department of the Aveyron, son of a notary who died young.

citation.chapter: EMILE POUGET'S LIFE AS AN ACTIVIST
citation.quote: Émile Pouget was born in 1860 near Rodez in the department of the Aveyron. His notary father died young.

title: Reversion toward the 1830 regime begins
summary: Proudhon identifies November 24, 1860 as the starting point of a political reversion to the regime of 1830, with the Bonaparte dynasty taking the role of the Bourbons.

citation.quote: Everything that has been done since November 24, 1860, in government and in opposition, indicates a reversion to the regime of 1830, with the sole modification that the title of emperor is to replace that of king, and the Bonaparte dynasty replace that of the Bourbons.

title: Bakunin escapes Siberia and reaches London
summary: After lengthy incarceration in Russia, Bakunin successfully escaped from Siberia in 1861 and made his way to London.

citation.chapter: THE REVOLUTION OF FEBRUARY 1848, AS SEEN BY BAKUNIN'
citation.quote: Then, in 1861, he successfully escaped from Siberia and made his way to London.

title: Le Peuple society launched in Belgium
summary: De Paepe joins with Voglet, Steens and others to launch the Le Peuple (People) society, a militant democratic association that would give rise to the Belgian section of the International Working Men's Association.

citation.chapter: DIRECT ACTION AND LIBERTARIAN CONSTRUCTION FORESHADOWED
citation.quote: He joined the Société des Solidaires (Fellowship Society) before joining with some new friends who included Voglet and Steens to launch the Le Peuple (People) society in 1861: this was a militant democratic association from which the Belgian section of the International Working Men's Association was to emerge four years later.

title: Guillaume travels to Zurich to study
summary: In September 1862, Guillaume traveled to Zurich to read philosophy, complete his education, and train as a teacher of Classics, enrolling at the philological and pedagogical institute run by Köchly.

citation.quote: In September 1862, Guillaume traveled up to Zurich; he was to read philosophy, complete his education, and train as a teacher of Classics. He enrolled at the philological and pedagogical institute run by Köchly.

title: Proudhon publishes Sworn Democrats and Refractories
summary: Proudhon led an abstentionist committee that produced meetings, handbills, posters, a manifesto, and on the eve of the election, his pamphlet Sworn Democrats and Refractories arguing against participation in imperial elections.

citation.quote: He was the driving force behind an abstentionist committee whose activity was intense: meetings, handbills, posters, all crowned by a cracking manifesto, and publication, on the eve of the election, of a pamphlet bearing his name and entitled Sworn Democrats and Refractories.

title: Jules Ferry publishes The Election Contest of 1863
summary: Jules Ferry, spokesman for the bourgeois democracy, published a pamphlet entitled The Election Contest of 1863, in which he ignored the worker candidates entirely.

citation.quote: The bourgeois democracy looked upon these candidacies with such contempt that its spokesman, Jules Ferry, in his pamphlet The Election Contest of 1863, quite simply passed over them without a mention.

title: Polish uprising against the tsarist empire
summary: The Polish uprising against the tsarist empire took place from 1863 to 1864, after which Bakunin became an anarchist.

citation.chapter: THE REVOLUTION OF FEBRUARY 1848, AS SEEN BY BAKUNIN'
citation.quote: It was after the uprising in Poland against the tsarist empire (1863–1864) and, doubtless, more especially after the conversations that he had with Proudhon...

title: Bakunin attempts to support Polish uprising
summary: When the Polish uprising erupted in 1863, Bakunin attempted to reach the activists leading it, but the Russian Legion failed and Lapinski's expedition came to nothing.

citation.chapter: THE REVOLUTION OF FEBRUARY 1848, AS SEEN BY BAKUNIN'
citation.quote: When the Polish uprising erupted in 1863, he [Bakunin] attempted to reach the activists leading it: but the organization of a Russian Legion failed, and Lapinski's expedition came to nothing

title: Proudhon publishes The Federal Principle
summary: Proudhon authored The Federal Principle in 1863, just two years before Bakunin's 'Program,' using the word 'State' in a federalistic, anti-centralistic sense.

citation.quote: And yet the later Proudhon, the author of *The Federal* *Principle* (1863), a book written just two years before Bakunin's "Program," also unashamedly uses the word "State" in the same federalistic, anti-centralistic sense with which Bakunin invests the term.

title: Polish Uprising
summary: Bakunin rushed to the assistance of the Polish Uprising; at the time he still supported Napoleon III, whose nationality principle he later criticized.

citation.quote: ...criticizing the nationality principle so dear to Napoleon III (whom Bakunin* *still supported at the time that he had rushed to the assistance of the Polish Uprising* *of* 1863).

title: General elections under Napoleon III's Empire
summary: The imperial regime held general elections on May 31 and June 1, 1863, the first electoral consultation since 1857. In Paris, democrats won a considerable majority of 153,000 votes to 82,000.

citation.quote: When the imperial regime held general elections on May 31 and June 1, 1863, there had been no consultation of the electorate since 1857.

title: Paris election night and lunar eclipse
summary: On the evening of June 1, 1863, as Paris celebrated the opposition's electoral victory, an eclipse of the moon occurred from 9:56 PM to 1:16 AM, seen by wits as despotism being eclipsed by liberty.

citation.quote: Monday, June 1, 1863, around ten in the evening: Paris is in the grip of a muffled agitation, reminiscent of that of July 26, 1830 and February 22, 1848.

title: Bakunin returns to London from Stockholm
summary: After unsuccessful attempts in Stockholm to get the Swedes to intervene in Poland, Bakunin returned to London in October.

citation.chapter: THE REVOLUTION OF FEBRUARY 1848, AS SEEN BY BAKUNIN'
citation.quote: Bakunin, who had gone to Stockholm (where his wife joined him) in hope of getting the Swedes to intervene, had to return to London (in October) without having succeeded in any of his ventures.

title: Bakunin meets Proudhon in Paris
summary: Bakunin had conversations with Proudhon in Paris towards the end of 1864, shortly before Proudhon's death, after which Bakunin became an anarchist.

citation.chapter: THE REVOLUTION OF FEBRUARY 1848, AS SEEN BY BAKUNIN'
citation.quote: more especially after the conversations that he had with Proudhon–a Proudhon whose death was not far off–in Paris towards the end of 1864, that Bakunin became an anarchist.

title: Bakunin makes second trip to Sweden
summary: In mid-1864, Bakunin made a second trip to Sweden from Italy, returning via London where he called on Marx and Paris where he called on Proudhon.

citation.chapter: THE REVOLUTION OF FEBRUARY 1848, AS SEEN BY BAKUNIN'
citation.quote: He then traveled to Italy, from where, in mid–1864, he made a second trip to Sweden: he returned via London, where he called again on Marx, and Paris, where he paid another call on Proudhon.

title: Bakunin stays in Italy and founds International Brotherhood
summary: Bakunin stayed in Italy until autumn 1867 (Florence, Naples), recruiting Italians, French, Scandinavians and Slavs into his secret society, the 'International Brotherhood' or 'Alliance of Socialist Revolutionaries.'

citation.chapter: THE REVOLUTION OF FEBRUARY 1848, AS SEEN BY BAKUNIN'
citation.quote: Bakunin stayed in the country until the autumn of 1867, staying first in Florence and then in Naples and its environs... from 1864 onwards, he managed to recruit a certain number of Italians, French, Scandinavians and Slavs into that secret society, which he dubbed the "International Brotherhood" or the "Alliance of Socialist Revolutionaries."

title: Guillaume publishes French translation of Gottfried Keller
summary: Guillaume was the first person ever to render Swiss writer Gottfried Keller's The Folk from Sedlwyla into French; his translation appeared in 1864.

citation.quote: Guillaume was the first person ever to render Keller into French and his book appeared in 1864.

title: Guillaume returns to Neuchatel
summary: In the spring of 1864, Guillaume was obliged to return to Neuchatel, having to abandon plans to make a study visit to Paris.

citation.quote: In the spring of 1864, Guillaume was obliged to return to Neuchatel.

title: Publication of Proudhon's On the Political Capacity of the Working Classes
summary: Proudhon's On the Political Capacity of the Working Classes was published.

citation.quote: See On the Political Capacity of the Working Classes, 1864.

title: Fanelli becomes friend and collaborator of Bakunin
summary: Giuseppe Fanelli became a friend and collaborator of Bakunin from 1864.

citation.quote: he became a friend and collaborator of Bakunin from 1864.

title: Eccarius joins the International in London
summary: From 1864, Hans Georg Eccarius was a member of the International in London.

citation.quote: then, from 1864, in London, of the International

title: Birth of Max Nettlau
summary: Max Nettlau, born in Vienna, the indefatigable historian of anarchism, was born.

citation.quote: Max Nettlau (1864–1944), born in Vienna, but of German nationality, the indefatigable historian and historiographer of anarchism

title: International General Council based in London
summary: The International's General Council was based in London from 1864 to 1872 before being moved to New York at the decision of the Hague congress.

citation.quote: The International's General Council, which had been based in London from 1864 to 1872, was removed, at the decision of the congress of The Hague, to New York, where Marx and Engels were counting upon finding compliant servants of their wishes.

title: Cipriani takes part in launch of the First International in London
summary: Italian libertarian revolutionary Amilcare Cipriani took part in the launch of the First International in London in 1864.

citation.quote: took part, in London, in the launch of the First International in 1864 and participated in the Paris Commune.

title: Manifesto of the Sixty workers published
summary: A 60-member workers' committee published the Manifesto of the Sixty in support of Tolain's candidacy. The text is regarded as the first public expression of working class consciousness in France.

citation.quote: MANIFESTO OF SIXTY WORKERS FROM THE SEINE DEPARTMENT (FEBRUARY I7, 1864)

title: Proudhon writes his Letter to Workers from Passy
summary: From Passy, Proudhon wrote his open letter responding to the Manifesto of the Sixty, urging workers to maintain abstention and reject worker candidacies under the imperial regime.

citation.quote:
PROUDHON'S LETTER TO WORKERS
